client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I sit down to try to get work done, these memories of her just come rushing in and I can't focus on anything else. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help — it feels like nothing can really fix what's missing.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're carrying right now is a profound grief, and it makes complete sense that her memory keeps breaking through when you try to focus, because she clearly meant so much to you. I notice that even as you're speaking about this, there's a kind of exhausted heaviness underneath your words, like you've been holding this pain tightly for a while now. You're right that nothing can "fix" what's missing, and I want you to know that's not what we're here to do — instead, we can gently explore what you're thinking and feeling so that grief has somewhere to go, rather than quietly blocking everything else in your life.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think "exhausted" is probably the right word for it. I've been trying to just push through everything — work, daily stuff — like if I keep moving, maybe it won't catch up to me. But it always does, usually at the worst times, like when I'm in the middle of a meeting or trying to fall asleep.
therapist: What you're describing — this strategy of staying in constant motion to outrun the grief — makes a lot of sense as a way to cope, but it sounds like your mind and body are gently, persistently reminding you that it's still there waiting. There's something telling in the way you're speaking right now, softly and carefully, like part of you is already tired of carrying this alone. In CBT, we'd gently examine that belief that "if I keep moving, it won't catch up" — because the evidence you're sharing suggests the grief is actually finding you *anyway*, and the cost of pushing through might be adding exhaustion on top of loss.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right, but the idea of just... stopping and letting it catch up to me feels genuinely terrifying. Like if I sit still long enough to actually feel it, I won't be able to function at all, and I can't afford that right now. I have too many responsibilities, people depending on me, so slowing down feels like a luxury I don't get to have.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — and I want to gently offer a different perspective on it: the belief that feeling your grief will cause you to fall apart and fail everyone depending on you is understandable, but it may not be the full truth. What's interesting is that even as you're speaking quickly, pushing through this explanation, your voice carries a quiet fragility underneath — like the very act of holding everything together is already costing you enormously. Allowing yourself to feel grief, even in small, contained moments, doesn't have to mean losing function — in fact, it might be what's quietly draining the energy you need to show up for all those responsibilities.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but I honestly don't know how I'd do that in a "contained" way. Like, where does grief start and where does it stop? I'm scared that if I open that door even a little, everything I've been holding back just floods out and I can't close it again.
therapist: That fear of being completely overwhelmed — of opening a door you can't close — is one of the most common and understandable fears in grief, and I can hear in your voice right now a real tension, almost like you're bracing yourself just talking about it. What I want you to know is that the "flood" you're imagining is actually a thought about grief, not grief itself — and our minds tend to catastrophize that moment of opening as far more destructive than it usually is in reality. We wouldn't dive into the deep end all at once; instead, we'd work together to build small, safe containers — maybe just five minutes of intentional reflection with a clear stopping point — so you can slowly learn that you *can* feel this and still come back to yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that it won't be as bad as I'm imagining. But honestly, the idea of even five minutes of intentionally sitting with all of this feels like agreeing to poke a sleeping bear — like, what if five minutes turns into five hours and I can't stop? I guess I just don't fully trust that I have the ability to pull myself back once I start going there.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with a kind of tightness in your voice — tells me that even *imagining* this feels activating and scary, and I want to acknowledge that what you're really expressing is a deep distrust of your own ability to regulate yourself. That's such an important thing to name, because the core belief underneath — "I can't trust myself to come back once I go there" — is actually something we can gently test over time, rather than just accept as fact. You've already been doing something incredibly hard this whole conversation: you've been touching the edges of this grief *right now*, and you're still here, still functioning, still finding words — which is quiet evidence that you have more capacity than you're giving yourself credit for.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but another part of me thinks... this conversation is controlled, you know? Like, I'm sitting here in a safe room with you, and of course I can find words here. But what about when I'm alone at 2am and it just hits me out of nowhere — that's when I completely fall apart, and no one's there to see that version of me.
therapist: That 2am version of you — alone, falling apart where no one can see — sounds like the loneliest, most unwitnessed part of this whole experience, and I can hear in your voice right now, even as you're speaking quickly, a kind of quiet ache around carrying that alone. You're right that this space is safer, and that's actually worth something — because what we practice here, these small ways of orienting yourself when the grief surges, are things you can begin to carry *into* those 2am moments over time. But I also want to gently reflect back: the fact that you just described that version of yourself so clearly, with such awareness, suggests that even in your hardest moments, some part of you is still observing, still present — and that part of you is more capable than you realize.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but honestly it feels a little... I don't know, too neat? Like, yes, I can describe it clearly right now, sitting here in the daylight, but at 2am that "observing part" you're talking about doesn't feel capable at all — it just feels like another voice piling on, watching me fall apart and doing nothing about it. I guess I'm skeptical that awareness in those moments is actually helping me rather than just making me more conscious of how alone I am.
therapist: That's a really honest and important pushback, and I don't want to dismiss it — because you're right that awareness without any sense of agency can feel less like a lifeline and more like a cruel witness. I notice you're speaking very quickly and softly right now, almost like you're rushing to get this out before something stops you, which tells me this particular fear — that nothing actually helps at 2am — is sitting very close to the surface. So let's not just talk about awareness as the answer; instead, let's work on building something more concrete — a small, specific thing you can *do* in those moments, not just observe, so that part of you has somewhere to go when it feels most alone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I mean... that actually lands a little differently than I expected. Like, I came in here ready to defend myself against another "just breathe and notice your thoughts" suggestion, and instead you're saying we build something I can actually do. But I'm also a little scared, because I've tried things before, little rituals or whatever, and at 2am when it's really bad, I just... I don't do them, I can't make myself, and then I feel worse because I had a plan and I still failed.
therapist: That moment of "I had a plan and I still failed" is such a painful layer on top of already being in pain — and I want to gently challenge the word "failed," because at 2am, exhausted and grieving and alone, not being able to execute a coping strategy isn't failure, it's just what overwhelming grief sometimes does. I can hear in your voice right now — soft, careful, like you're holding something fragile — that this fear of trying and falling short might actually be a bigger barrier than the grief itself at this point. So what if we designed something so small and so low-stakes that there's almost nothing to fail at — not a ritual that requires you to perform wellness, but just one tiny anchor that asks almost nothing of you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that reframe about failure... but another part of me is sitting here thinking, what's so small that it can't go wrong? Because even the idea of coming up with something feels like a task I could mess up. I guess that's kind of what you're pointing at, but it's hard to shake the feeling that even "tiny" becomes another thing on a list that proves I can't manage my own grief.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very quickly, softly, at a high pitch — tells me that even this conversation, this very moment of trying to figure out how to help yourself, is activating that same fear of getting it wrong. And I want to name something important: the thought "even coming up with something small is a task I could mess up" is the grief talking, not the truth about your capabilities — it's a mind that's exhausted and has learned to expect disappointment from itself. So what if, for now, the only thing we agree on is this: there is nothing to come up with today, nothing to implement, no list — just the fact that you showed up here and kept talking honestly, which is already more than "not managing."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but there's this other part that immediately goes "okay, but showing up isn't actually enough, is it?" Like, my mom is still gone, and I'm still going home to that empty apartment tonight, and nothing about this hour changes that. I don't want to dismiss what you're offering, I just... I guess I'm scared that if I let myself feel like I did something good today, I'll wake up tomorrow and the grief will just be waiting there anyway, unchanged.
therapist: You're absolutely right that the grief will be there tomorrow — I won't pretend otherwise — and there's something deeply honest and courageous in the way you're saying that, even as I can hear a kind of quiet exhaustion underneath the speed of your words, like you're bracing for disappointment before it even arrives. But I want to gently separate two things: the grief being there tomorrow is true, and *also* today meaning something can be true — those don't cancel each other out, even though your mind is working very hard right now to make them feel mutually exclusive. You didn't come here to fix grief today; you came here and told the truth about how hard it is, and that's not nothing — that's actually the very first thread we pull to slowly, slowly make the weight a little more bearable over time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
